title: AP 2-D Art and Design
summary: Investigate composition, visual relationships and documented revision in two-dimensional work.
frameworkNote: Checked against the official course page on 15 October 2026 for 2026-27. This is an original four-part portfolio skill sequence across inquiry, making and presentation, not prescribed College Board units. Text exercises support planning and reflection; they do not create, assess or certify a portfolio. Check current submission and AI rules with your teacher.

modules.title: Turn an observation into an inquiry
modules.focus: Ask a question that can change through visual experiments.
explanation: A subject names what appears in an image; an inquiry asks what you want to discover by making it. “Bus stops” is a subject. “How can repeated rectangles suggest waiting?” connects observation to a visual decision and leaves room for different answers.

Collect your own observational sketches and note where, when and why you made them. Separate an influence from a source image. If you use another person’s material, record its origin and permissions, then follow current portfolio rules. A visual inquiry should develop through your decisions rather than a prewritten explanation pasted onto finished work.

workedExample.prompt: Develop an inquiry from three sketches of an empty station.
steps: Identify a recurring relationship: large gaps between small figures.
Ask how changing scale and negative space affects the sense of isolation. Plan two compositions to compare.

misconception.claim: A portfolio needs one unchanging answer.
misconception.correction: An inquiry can become more specific as experiments reveal new visual possibilities.

questions.prompt: Rewrite “I like flowers” as a testable visual inquiry.
questions.hint: Choose a relationship such as repetition or scale.
questions.answer: One possibility: How can repeated petal shapes create movement across a static page?
checkpoints: Names a visual variable
Allows more than one experiment

questions.hint: Consider what a later viewer could learn from it.
questions.answer: It can show a compositional decision and why the next version changed, if the annotation identifies that change.
checkpoints: Connects evidence to revision

questions.prompt: Turn 'I enjoy maps' into a visual inquiry about belonging.
questions.answer: Ask how erasing borders changes a map's sense of belonging. Compare versions with different border visibility. Assess how routes and regions become connected or separated.
checkpoints: Ask how erasing borders changes a map's sense of belonging.
Compare versions with different border visibility.

questions.prompt: A beautiful colour study does not affect later work. How can it become useful investigation evidence?
questions.hint: Connect the test to a decision.
hints: Connect the test to a decision.
questions.answer: Identify the colour relationship tested. Show how it informed or challenged a later choice. If it had no relevant effect, do not present it as decisive evidence.

notes.title: Turn an observation into an inquiry in depth
paragraphs: A visual inquiry becomes productive when it links an idea to a relationship that can change on the page. Start with something observed, then vary a specific feature such as overlap, colour temperature or edge density. The question should invite several possible outcomes rather than prescribe one finished image. Compare tests using the intended experience, not simply which looks most polished. An unsuccessful experiment can clarify the inquiry when its annotation identifies what the visible result revealed and why the next choice followed.

workedExamples.prompt: Develop an inquiry from overlapping window reflections.
steps: Notice that reflected figures merge with interior objects.
Test transparent layers against opaque silhouettes while keeping the window frame constant.
workedExamples.conclusion: Ask how layered visibility can make public and private spaces seem to overlap.

flashcards.back: It can be investigated through material or compositional choices.

flashcards.front: Is polish the same as investigation?
flashcards.back: No; a rough test may reveal more.

flashcards.front: What should a rejected test record?
flashcards.back: What failed and how that shaped revision.

modules.title: Organise hierarchy and balance
modules.focus: Use scale, value and placement to direct attention.
explanation: Visual hierarchy is the order in which elements attract attention. Contrast, size, isolation and directional lines can make one shape dominant. Balance describes how visual weight is distributed; an asymmetrical arrangement can feel stable without matching shapes on each side.

Make small thumbnails before polishing detail. Reduce a composition to three values and inspect whether the intended focal area still reads. A bright colour may dominate because of saturation, while a dark shape may dominate because of area. Explain the actual relationship in your image rather than treating a principle as a universal recipe.

workedExample.prompt: A poster has three equally large, dark circles. Make one the focal point.
steps: Keep two circles smaller and closer together.
Separate the third circle with more surrounding light space, then compare where the eye lands first.

misconception.correction: Unequal shapes can balance through placement, contrast and visual weight.

questions.prompt: A tiny red square competes with a large grey rectangle. Name two variables to test.
questions.answer: Test saturation and isolation, keeping other features constant enough to compare the effect.
checkpoints: Names two visual properties
Describes a comparison

questions.prompt: How could a crop change emphasis without adding anything?
questions.answer: Cropping away empty space can enlarge a subject relative to the frame and remove competing detail.
checkpoints: Links crop to hierarchy
Explains a visible effect

questions.prompt: A poster's heading and image compete equally. Propose a specific hierarchy revision.
questions.hint: Choose which must be read first.
hints: Choose which must be read first.
questions.answer: Make the heading the primary element. Reduce the image's contrast or scale. Check that the image now supports rather than interrupts the reading order.
checkpoints: Make the heading the primary element.
Reduce the image's contrast or scale.
Check that the image now supports rather than interrupts the reading order.

questions.prompt: Explain how an off-centre black square can balance a larger pale rectangle.
questions.hint: Consider value as well as size.
hints: Consider value as well as size.
questions.answer: Dark value can give the smaller square substantial visual weight. Distance from the centre affects its balance with the rectangle. The whole arrangement must be assessed, not area alone.
checkpoints: Dark value can give the smaller square substantial visual weight.
Distance from the centre affects its balance with the rectangle.
The whole arrangement must be assessed, not area alone.

notes.title: Organise hierarchy and balance in depth
paragraphs: Visual hierarchy directs attention through relationships rather than isolated features. A large shape may dominate, but a small high-contrast mark can compete with it. Balance concerns the distribution of visual weight; it does not require mirror symmetry. Test a composition at thumbnail scale to see whether the primary relationships remain readable before adding detail. Changes in spacing can alter both emphasis and rhythm. Explain which relationship you intend viewers to notice first and how secondary elements support or complicate that route.

workedExamples.prompt: Make a pale doorway the focus in a dark, crowded collage.
steps: Reserve the lightest value for the doorway and reduce competing light patches.
Arrange smaller dark fragments so their edges direct attention towards the opening.
workedExamples.conclusion: Value contrast and directional placement reinforce the same focal area.

flashcards.back: No; unequal elements can balance through visual weight.

diagrams.title: Doorway emphasis
diagrams.description: Two choices cooperate to direct attention.

nodes.label: Directed viewing
nodes.detail: Surrounding edges lead towards the opening.

modules.title: Revise a material experiment
modules.focus: Connect process changes to a visual purpose.
explanation: Experimentation compares possibilities. Revision uses what the comparison reveals to change a work. In a collage, transparent paper, torn edges and repeated photocopies affect layering in different ways. Document which materials you tested and why their behaviour matters to your inquiry.

Avoid changing every feature at once if you need to understand a particular effect. You might hold the arrangement constant while varying opacity. Later, combine useful discoveries in a new composition. A failed transfer can become evidence of learning, but merely labelling it “experimental” does not explain what you discovered.

workedExample.prompt: A layered street collage looks flat despite five paper layers.
steps: Compare opaque and translucent versions of the same overlap.
Keep the version that reveals depth and revise edge contrast so the foreground remains legible.

misconception.claim: More materials automatically demonstrate more skill.
misconception.correction: Material choices matter when their properties contribute to the intended visual relationship.

questions.prompt: What should an annotation say about a smudged print?
questions.answer: The wet ink spread into the next shape; letting the plate dry longer made the boundary clearer in the next print.
checkpoints: Names the process
Connects revision to observation

questions.prompt: Design a fair comparison of two textures.
questions.answer: Use the same shape, scale and light-dark relationship, then compare rough and smooth surfaces for the intended emphasis.
checkpoints: Holds useful variables steady
States the purpose

questions.prompt: A watercolour spreads beyond a planned boundary. Give a useful next test.
questions.answer: Compare the same shape on damp and dry paper. Record how moisture changes the edge. Choose the condition that supports the intended clarity or diffusion.
checkpoints: Compare the same shape on damp and dry paper.
Record how moisture changes the edge.
Choose the condition that supports the intended clarity or diffusion.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I used more materials' not evidence of stronger development?
questions.answer: Additional materials do not automatically deepen an inquiry. The artist must show their visual effect. That effect must connect to a reasoned decision or question.
checkpoints: Additional materials do not automatically deepen an inquiry.
The artist must show their visual effect.
That effect must connect to a reasoned decision or question.

notes.title: Revise a material experiment in depth
paragraphs: Material experiments are meaningful when the procedure and visual purpose are linked. Record enough about pressure, dilution, drying time or layering to understand why the outcome changed. A test need not isolate every variable scientifically, but changing many features at once makes attribution difficult. Compare evidence of the surface, including edges and unintended marks, before deciding whether an accident serves the inquiry. Revision can preserve an unexpected effect while altering its placement or intensity so that it contributes deliberately to the work.

workedExamples.prompt: A monoprint intended to suggest fog has sharp, uniform edges.
steps: Compare a lightly wiped plate with the original to soften selected boundaries.
Retain one crisp foreground edge so the depth does not disappear entirely.
workedExamples.conclusion: Selective softness suggests obscured distance more effectively than making every edge equally vague.

flashcards.back: They help explain and repeat an effect.
No; it may serve the inquiry.

flashcards.front: Why avoid changing everything at once?
flashcards.back: The source of an effect becomes unclear.
A visible change connected to intended meaning.

diagrams.description: Different edges establish a spatial relationship.

modules.title: Present evidence of decisions
modules.focus: Sequence work and write concrete process statements.
explanation: A presentation should let a viewer inspect relationships between works, not just read claims about them. Select images that show development, including a meaningful detail or intermediate state when it explains a change. Photograph flat work evenly so shadows and colour casts do not misrepresent it.

A process statement connects an intention, a choice and an observed result. “I moved the darkest shape to the edge to make the route feel interrupted” is more useful than “I used contrast well.” Keep authorship and source records clear. These text exercises cannot substitute for the actual images or your own required written responses.

workedExample.prompt: Improve the statement “My collage is about memory and is effective.”
steps: Identify a visible choice: repeated fragments become less legible across the page.
Explain how fading and overlap suggest incomplete recall, then name the revision that strengthened that effect.

misconception.claim: A strong statement can compensate for missing visual evidence.
misconception.correction: The images must show the decisions the statement describes.

questions.prompt: Which image belongs beside a final collage: an unrelated sketch or an opacity test? Why?
questions.answer: The opacity test belongs if its result explains the layering used in the final collage.
checkpoints: Selects relevant evidence
Explains the connection

questions.prompt: Name two checks before photographing a flat work.
questions.answer: Keep the camera parallel to the surface and use even lighting that avoids glare or strong shadows.
checkpoints: Checks alignment
Checks lighting

questions.prompt: Revise 'I made the picture better' for a composition with reduced background contrast.
questions.answer: I reduced the background's light-dark contrast. This made the figure's outline more prominent. The change directs attention to the figure before the setting.
checkpoints: I reduced the background's light-dark contrast.
This made the figure's outline more prominent.
The change directs attention to the figure before the setting.

questions.prompt: Why include dimensions beside a collage photograph?
questions.answer: The photograph alone does not establish physical size. Dimensions distinguish intimate from large-scale viewing. That scale affects how texture and detail are encountered.
checkpoints: The photograph alone does not establish physical size.
Dimensions distinguish intimate from large-scale viewing.
That scale affects how texture and detail are encountered.

notes.title: Present evidence of decisions in depth
paragraphs: Documentation should make the work and its development understandable without replacing visual evidence with claims. Sequence selected tests so that a viewer can follow consequential decisions, not merely chronological activity. Process statements should name an observable change and explain its purpose. Photograph flat work with controlled lighting and a parallel camera to reduce distortion, and distinguish a detail view from a full view. Accurate materials and dimensions help viewers interpret surface and scale; an image edited to conceal defects can misrepresent the actual work.

workedExamples.prompt: Sequence three invented images of a fragmented portrait.
steps: Begin with the intact study, then show the test where fragments obscure every feature.
End with the revision retaining one eye to anchor recognition.
workedExamples.conclusion: The sequence shows how selective fragmentation balanced disruption with identification.

flashcards.front: What should a process statement name?
flashcards.back: A visible decision and its reason.
It does not represent the whole composition.
A camera angled away from the flat surface.
